F01:
*If you have been here before,* the perfume barely reaches you now, and the Food Court's yellow light has crept a table nearer the arch. Go straight to the choices.

Otherwise:

Under the arch from the Atrium, the perfume closes round you.

Sweet and expensive, a hundred testers sighing. Every counter is lit. Behind each one stands an empty stool with a folded cardigan on the seat.

Under the sweetness is a cleaner, sharper smell. Alcohol gel. Floor polish. The hush of a corridor where people lower their voices because of the room at the end of it.

Home and hospital, both at once. Your throat closes.

*If Sam is with you,* the smell reaches him a second after you. He stops and sneezes, twice, hard. "Every time," he says, wiping his nose. "Dad said I was allergic to anything over a tenner." He walks on, glaring at the testers.

Ahead, the shop runs back between tall mirrored pillars. To your left, past a row of dead tills, the Food Court glows yellow, and fat is spitting on a hot plate. By the arch, a coffee kiosk has its shutter down, and a curl of white paper has spilled out from under it across the floor.

Somewhere among the shelves, a tester hisses once, all by itself.

If you go deeper into the Duty-Free shop, turn to {F02}.

If you follow the smell of cooking to the Food Court, turn to {F15}.

If you haven't already looked at the till at the closed kiosk by the arch, turn to {F33}.
F33:
The kiosk's shutter stops a few inches short of the counter. The till roll has come out through the gap, and it has kept coming.

It runs off the counter, down the front of the kiosk and across the floor in loose white loops. Metres of it, and none of it torn off.

You pick up the end nearest your feet. The print is faint purple, the old kind of till ink.

*LARKVALE CATERING   KIOSK 3*
*14/03/1987   23:58*
*2  CHEESE TOASTIE*
*1  TEA*
*1  HOT CHOC*
*THANK YOU FOR WAITING*

A family's order, line for line. If you ate at the gate tonight, you know whose.

The next receipt along is the same. Same date, same minute. And the next. You follow the loops back towards the kiosk, paper sliding over your wrist, and somewhere in the loops the date changes.

*23/11/1998   23:58.* Two cheese toasties. A tea. A hot chocolate. Over and over, the ink darker, the paper whiter.

The last receipt hangs from the slot under the shutter. The ink is wet enough to smudge at a touch, and the date on it is tonight's.

1987. 1998. Tonight. Always 23:58.

*If Sam is with you,* he leans over your arm and taps the 1987. "Neither of us was born," he says. He moves down to *HOT CHOC*. "That was always mine." He lets the paper drop.

Behind the shutter, in the dark, the till gives a small electric click, and the paper moves forward one line.

You let the loops fall and step back over them to the arch.

Turn to {F01}.
F02:
*If you have been here before,* your reflection is already in the pillar, ahead of you. Go straight to the choices.

The mirrored pillars go back further than the shop should allow.

Spirits. Cigarette cartons in wrappers nearly thirty years out of date. Chocolate in tins the size of hatboxes. And between the aisles, floor-to-ceiling mirrors, so that wherever you look you're looking at yourself between bottles.

You walk, and your reflection walks with you.

Almost with you. It's a fraction late, the gap on a bad phone line when your own voice comes back a beat after you've spoken. You lift an arm to test it. The one in the glass lifts after yours, slow and sleepy.

You keep it up longer than you meant to.

Two aisles over, a stand of sunglasses turns on its spindle, squeaking once on every lap.

*If Sam is with you,* he's the one spinning it, idly, not looking up. He hasn't noticed the pillars. You decide not to make him.

There's a row of perfume testers on a glass shelf, and among them a squat green bottle you'd know anywhere. There's a newspaper stand by the till. There's the nearest mirror. And at the back, past the whisky, a grey door marked STAFF ONLY.

In the pillar beside you, your reflection lowers its arm. You lowered yours a while ago.

If you try the perfume testers, turn to {F03}.

If you step up to the mirror and study it, turn to {F04}.

If you haven't already looked at the newspapers, turn to {F28}.

If you head for the STAFF ONLY door at the back, turn to {F08}.
F03:
The testers stand in a row on little chains. Most you don't know. One you'd know in the dark: squat green glass, a black cap with a dent worn into it by a thumb that isn't here any more.

You press the nozzle once against the inside of your wrist.

And you're nine, in the back of his car.

Rain. The wipers going *thunk, thunk*. The heater smells of hot dust, and over all of it the smell of him, because he's put too much on again. In the rear-view mirror his eyes find yours.

*Not long now, Kite.*

You were going to the viewing deck. You were always going to the viewing deck.

The smell brings the other one too, the one you didn't ask for. A Sunday call, a year and a half ago, his voice bright and careful. *Bit of news, Kite. Don't go mad.*

Sam had already driven him to every appointment. *Didn't want you worrying,* Dad said. *Not over there. Not on your own.*

You come to in the shop. Your wrist is pressed under your nose. In the glass of the shelf, your reflection hasn't opened its eyes. Gain 1 Fear.

Behind you, a stand of sunglasses squeaks once around its spindle and stops.

Turn to {F05}.
F05:
The sunglasses stand squeaks to a stop in front of you.

It's the stupidest rack in the building. White plastic stars with pink lenses. Leopard print. A pair of red hearts, enormous, with the price sticker still on one lobe. Right at the bottom, a row of gold aviators.

You put the hearts on. In the mirrored pillar a stranger in red hearts looks back, deadly serious, and you laugh. It hurts on the way out. Your father is nine days dead and you are wearing hearts in an empty airport.

Dad wore aviators in the hospital. He told you so himself, on one of the Sunday calls you did pick up. *The nurses call me the Captain. Captain of the viewing deck.* You laughed. He'd wanted you to.

*If Sam is with you,* he's already in the white stars, chin up, a film star at the top of the aircraft steps. "Well?" And he laughs, the old one that starts in his shoulders, and holds on to the stand so he doesn't fall over. "Worst band in the world." Then: "He said he'd take his off when you turned up."

The stand squeaks once more. Nobody touches it. Gain 2 Vigour.

In the mirrored pillar, long after you've stopped, your reflection is still laughing.

If Sam is with you and you do not have the codeword TOLD, and you tell him the truth about the hospital, here, now, turn to {F29}.

If you laugh it off and move on, turn to {F08}.
F29:
"It wasn't work."

You're still wearing the hearts. You can't take them off now. It would be worse.

"I said work. To everyone. To you. Next month. Flights are mad. Next month." Your voice keeps going without you. "I had the leave. I booked it. March. I got to the gate, Sam."

The stand squeaks round once.

"I had the pass in my hand. And I turned round. I went home."

He doesn't move. Behind the pink lenses you can't see his eyes.

"I couldn't watch him. Get small. Go. I couldn't, so I didn't, so you did." You run out of sentence. "All of it. I let you."

Sam takes off the stars. He folds the arms in, one, two, and puts them back on the stand the right way up.

"He asked for you. Every day." He swallows. "I told him you were busy."

"Sam—"

"Busy. I got good at busy. Busy, bad line, your flight's moved. Busy."

He looks at the stand, not at you, for a long time.

"And I didn't exactly ask you to come, did I." He picks at the arm of the stars. "So."

He nods at the hearts. "Take those off. I can't do this with you in those."

*If you have the codeword TRUCE,* he gets there first. He reaches over, takes them off your face, carefully, and folds them beside the stars. "There," he says. "Now I can see you."

*Otherwise,* you take the hearts off yourself and fold them beside the stars.

He walks on, down the far side of the aisle, his knuckles knocking softly along the bottles.

Lose 2 Fear. Note the codeword TOLD.

At the back of the shop, past the whisky, the grey STAFF ONLY door stands ajar. It was shut when you came in.

Turn to {F08}.
F28:
The newspapers by the till are bundled in plastic ties, straight off the van. You hook a nail under a tie and it snaps.

The date on the masthead is tomorrow's.

The front page is ordinary. Weather. A strike. A footballer's knee. That's the worst of it. You turn the pages, and on page four, at the bottom, under an advert for garden furniture:

*TWO MORE MISSING AT GATE 0*

*If you are his son:* Beneath it, smaller: *BROTHERS WERE FLYING HOME FOR FATHER'S FUNERAL.*

*If you are his daughter:* Beneath it, smaller: *BROTHER AND SISTER WERE FLYING HOME FOR FATHER'S FUNERAL.*

*If neither:* Beneath it, smaller: *SIBLINGS WERE FLYING HOME FOR FATHER'S FUNERAL.*

The story is short. Two passengers, last seen in the terminal overnight, booked on a delayed Larkvale Airways flight. No record of them leaving. *Their names bring the total to 139.* In 1998, the article reminds readers, all 137 passengers of flight LV 137 vanished from the same gate.

137 then. Tonight, two more.

There's a photograph, grainy, from a camera high above Gate 14. Two people on the hard plastic seats, one empty seat between them that neither has put a bag on. Gain 1 Fear.

You fold the paper and put it back. Every paper on the stand is the same paper. On the top copy, the photograph has changed. Both small figures have turned. They're looking up, into the camera.

Turn to {F02}.
F04:
You step up to the nearest pillar, close enough to see the pores of your own face.

Your reflection steps up a moment later.

You watch it the way you'd watch a stranger on a train. It's you, down to the crease your bag strap has left in your jacket and the red where you've been rubbing at your face. *If you wear the UNIFORM,* it wears it too, the blank badge catching the light. It breathes when you breathe. Nearly.

You blink. It doesn't.

Its eyes stay open, drying, fixed on yours. Its mouth is moving. No sound comes through the glass, only the shape of two words, over and over. The first pushes the lips forward. The second presses them shut and opens them again.

You lean in to read them, and it leans in too, in time with you for once.

Behind it, the shop is the shop behind you, except that in the glass the STAFF ONLY door at the back stands wide open.

It lifts a hand and lays it flat on the inside of the mirror, at the height of yours, for you to match.

If you decide it's wrong and turn away, turn to {F06}.

If you tell yourself it's only tired eyes and lean closer, turn to {F07}.

If you reach out and touch the glass, turn to {D05}.
D05:
You lay your palm against its palm.

The glass is cool. Now the cool is in your wrist, your elbow, your collarbone, and when you pull back there's no back to pull to.

The shop turns over, and you're behind the glass. It's silver in here, and quiet, and you're the one who is late now. You lift an arm and the world takes its time to notice.

Out on the shop floor, it rolls your shoulders. Tries your face on. Picks up your bag.

*If Sam is with you,* it goes to find him first. You watch it in every pillar. Sam makes a joke about the sunglasses, and it laughs half a second early. At the arch Sam glances back at the mirrors and frowns. It claps him on the shoulder, which you never do, and he lets it.

It walks out under the arch towards the Atrium, sure of the way.

You press against the inside of the glass and wait for someone to match you.

Far off, a pen squeaks once against card.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {F02} and choose again.
F06:
You stumble back from the pillar and don't look at it again.

But there's glass everywhere in this shop. Cabinets, shelves, the cases where watches lie stopped on velvet. Whichever way you face, there's glass in front of you.

You lean on a display case, head down, gulping air. It fogs a soft grey oval on the glass under your face.

Letters come up in it.

They were written before, by someone leaning where you are, and left for someone's breath to find. Small capitals. Round and careful and steady:

*BEHIND THE WHISKY*

You keep huffing on the glass to hold the words there, until your lungs give out and they fade.

Someone came through here before you, and left the light on. Your shoulders come down from round your ears. Lose 1 Fear.

At the end of the whisky aisle, where the bottles stop and the bare wall starts, there's a grey door.

Turn to {F08}.
F07:
You lean closer. Tired eyes. A long night, bad light.

The glass gives.

It doesn't crack. It sags inward against your forehead, cold and wet, and its arm comes through and takes a fistful of your collar. Its knuckles are your knuckles. Its breath, an inch from your mouth, smells of nothing at all.

It pulls. The cold closes over one ear, and the shop goes muffled on that side, a swimming pool heard from underwater. You jam a foot against the base of the pillar, get a grip on its wrist, and haul back with everything you have. Its mouth keeps shaping the same two words.

REFLECTION   NERVE 7   VIGOUR 6

If you win, turn to {F06}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
F08:
The grey door at the back of the shop is the only thing in Duty-Free that isn't trying to sell you anything.

Scuffed paint at kicking height. A push plate worn silver in the middle by years of pushing. *STAFF ONLY*, in English and in a second script, which rearranges itself while you're still on the English. The last shelf of whisky stands right beside it.

The door is open a crack. Through it come hard white light and a radio, low, playing a pop song from the year you were six. The same chorus, over and over. When it reaches the end, it starts again mid-word.

Under the radio: a teaspoon going round a mug. A plastic chair creaking. Someone turning a page, slowly, then turning it back.

A break room. By the sound of it, the break has gone on for years.

You lay a hand on the push plate, and the radio stops in the middle of a word.

If you slip through quietly, turn to {F09}.

If you knock, turn to {F10}.
F09:
You ease the door open with your shoulder, just wide enough, and slide through sideways with your bag held against your chest.

*If Sam is with you,* he comes through close behind, lips pressed tight.

A narrow corridor. Strip lights. Lockers along one wall, each with a name on a strip of tape. On your left, a doorway spills yellow light and the smell of stewed tea. You can hear chairs in there. Breathing. The radio, back on, low.

The stockroom is at the far end. You go heel to toe, your bag pressed to your ribs, keeping to the edge where the floor should be firmest.

Halfway, the floor gives a long, considered creak.

The breathing in the break room stops.

Test your Fortune. If you are Lucky, turn to {F11}. If you are Unlucky, turn to {F12}.
F10:
You knock twice, politely, and wait.

"Come in," says a voice. Several voices, together, kindly.

The door gives onto a short corridor, lockers down one side, each with a name on a strip of tape. The voices come from a doorway on the left, and you go in. The break room is small and stuffy. A kettle. A fridge with a handwritten note about milk. A staff rota on a cork board, every shift crossed off up to 23/11/1998, and nothing after.

And the staff. Five or six of them in navy uniforms with red piping, sitting on plastic chairs pulled right up to the far wall, noses almost touching the paint. Their backs are straight. On the floor in front of each of them, a mug of tea has grown a skin. None of them turns round.

Across the room, a second door opens back onto the corridor, and at its far end is a door marked *STOCKROOM*.

The strip light overhead ticks. Stutters. Goes out, comes back, goes out.

In the dark between flickers, the plastic chairs creak together: the sound chairs make when the people in them start, slowly, to turn.

Rule 1. *Do not look at the passenger when the lights flicker.* These aren't passengers. You're almost sure.

If you keep your eyes on the floor and tiptoe past them to the stockroom, turn to {F11}.

If you look at them, turn to {F12}.
F11:
The stockroom door shuts behind you, and the rest of the airport goes quiet with it.

Metal shelving runs to the ceiling, stacked with cardboard boxes, each labelled in black marker with a name and a seat number. *A. OKAFOR 23F. M. LINDQVIST 9B. WALTER 14C.* It isn't stock. It's luggage that never got where it was going.

Yours is on a low shelf, your name typed on a luggage label. Inside: a pair of plastic pilot's wings. A kite with a snapped spar. A crayon aeroplane with three stick people at the windows, one window labelled in your six-year-old capitals: *SAM*.

*If Sam is with you,* he keeps his back against the door until he sees the box beside yours with his name on it. He looks at it a long time and doesn't open it. "Not yet," he says.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* Sam's box sits beside yours, taped shut, and far heavier than a box of toys should be.

At the back, behind the cases of whisky, a yellowed sheet is pinned to the wall under the Larkvale crest: *PASSENGER MANIFEST. LV 137. 1998.*

Names in seat order, two columns. Every name but one has a single line through it in the same blue ink. You count without meaning to. You lose count in the forties and start again, touching each line.

A hundred and thirty-seven lines.

One name has no line. Seat 1A. Your father's name. Beside it, in pencil: *DID NOT BOARD.*

*If you do not already have the LAST PAGE,* there is a torn page of typed text taped above the manifest. You peel it off the wall. Note the LAST PAGE on your Adventure Sheet.

Behind the last shelf, a fire door stands propped on a mop bucket. It lets you out among the perfume counters.

Turn to {F14}.
F12:
*If you chose to look at them,* you look. Every chair has turned towards you, and every chair is empty.

Something settles on your shoulder, light as a name badge.

"Excuse me."

They're all around you, though you never heard them move. Navy uniforms. Red piping. Larkvale wings on every lapel. Hair set and sprayed, out of photographs from when you were small. Every name badge has been left blank.

And all of them are saying sorry. A soft, continuous *sorry, sorry, so sorry* under their breath, never stopping for air.

*If Sam is with you,* two of them have him by the elbows against the wall, apologising into his ears.

"Shoplifting," says the one holding your shoulder, "is a serious matter."

You haven't taken anything. You open your mouth to say so, and your hand is in your jacket pocket, closed round a small cold bottle. A tester, squat and green. You don't remember picking it up.

"We'll just need your name," she says, "for the report." Her grip tightens. Her pen is already touching the form.

Over her shoulder, the stockroom door is six strides away. Behind you, the corridor back to the shop looks long.

If you break past her for the stockroom door, turn to {F13}.

If you twist out of her grip and run back the way you came, turn to {F24}.
F13:
You wrench free of her and go for the stockroom door.

The crew don't run. They don't need to. The strip lights stutter, and every time they come back the crew are closer.

You never see them move. A blank badge at your elbow, a lacquered head at the edge of your eye, polished nails already resting on the door frame ahead of you. *Sorry, sorry. If you'd just. Nearly done.*

*If Sam is with you,* he tears free of the wall and comes after you, swinging his backpack at anything navy. You hear him behind you, and then beside you.

Fingers catch your sleeve, your collar, the soft place under your jaw. You duck and twist and keep going. Six strides. Four. The lights go out again.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, you get past them and through the door before a single grip can close. If you fail, they get hold of you on the threshold, and you tear free bruised and shaking, with the marks of neat nails in your arms: lose 4 Vigour and gain 1 Fear.

Either way, turn to {F11}.
F24:
You drop your shoulder and twist, and she comes away holding nothing but the smell of your jacket.

You run for the shop.

Back down the corridor, past the taped names, out into the shop. *If Sam is with you,* he tore loose from the wall and got through the grey door ahead of you; he held it for you, and now he lets it slam. There are no footsteps behind you. There's only a voice, pleasant and unhurried, saying *passenger, passenger, please*, always the same distance back however fast you go.

The aisles have moved. The whisky is where the chocolate was. A pillar flashes a stranger at you, and the stranger is you, running.

Ahead, the yellow glow of the Food Court.

Test your Fortune. If you are Lucky, turn to {F15}. If you are Unlucky, turn to {F30}.
F30:
You're nearly clear when they catch the back of your jacket.

Fingernails. Several sets, short and neat and terribly strong. They drag from your shoulder blades to your waist, through your jacket and your shirt and into you. It doesn't hurt at first. It feels like being written on. Then it hurts.

You tear free and keep going.

*If Sam is with you,* he gets a fist in your collar and hauls you the last few steps.

Behind you a voice says, "Thank you, that'll be all," and the footsteps you never heard stop at the edge of the shop.

Your back is wet. You don't reach round to find out how wet. Lose 4 Vigour.

You stagger on towards the light and the smell of cooking, because it's the only way that isn't behind you.

Turn to {F15}.
F14:
*8. A pass carries every name its holder loves, once every debt is settled.*

One rule, by itself at the top of the page, in the same square typewriter letters as the Handbook, punched so hard the letters stand up from the back of the page. The torn edge is ragged and old. It would fit the stub left in the Handbook's staples.

*Every name its holder loves.*

*If Sam is with you,* you hold it out to him. He reads it, passes it back, and gives it one word. "Gamble."

Below the rule there's a gap. Then, much smaller, down in the corner where forms keep their small print:

*Transfer passengers know their number.*

That's all. The page ends there.

Far off, from the direction of the Atrium, the great board starts to clatter, every flap turning over.

You fold the page away and go back towards the Atrium.

Tick one hour on your Adventure Sheet.

If you have just ticked your sixth hour, turn to {E_FINALCALL}.

If you do not have RETURNED, turn to {H05}.

If you have RETURNED but not HEARD, turn to {H03}.

Otherwise turn to {H01}.
F15:
*If you have been here before,* the Chef is back at a hundred and four. Go straight to the choices.

Gravy. Fresh bread. Bacon on a Sunday. The Food Court smells of every good meal of your life, and your mouth floods so fast it hurts.

Every franchise counter has its shutter down but one. Behind it stands a Chef in a tall white hat, a navy uniform with red piping under his apron. He's ladling.

His lips move as he works. "A hundred and four," he's saying. "A hundred and five." One portion, one number.

His knuckles are white. Frost-white, as if he's held the inside of a freezer far too long.

The queue for his counter winds back between the tables and out of sight. Grey people in coats and haircuts from 1998, holding trays, shuffling one step at a time. At the tables, more of them, eating slowly, never finishing. The Delayed. Every one has a boarding pass gone the colour of tea.

*If Sam is with you,* his stomach growls, loud in the hush. He folds his arms over it. "Rule four," he says. "I know. I *know*." He has picked up a tray anyway.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* at one of the tables, in front of an empty chair, a hot chocolate is steaming.

By the far windows, a row of sleep pods glows a soft blue.

"A hundred and twelve," the Chef says. "A hundred and thirteen." The ladle stops over an empty plate, and he starts again. "One."

He looks up, finds you, and lifts the ladle in greeting.

If you take a tray and eat, turn to {F16}.

If you refuse to eat, turn to {F17}.

If you have the VOUCHER and give it to him, turn to {F18}.

If you go and rest in the sleep pods by the windows, turn to {F27}.
F16:
You don't queue. The Delayed step aside without looking up, and there's a plate waiting on the counter before you reach it, a stool pulled out in front of it.

Chips. Beans. A sausage cut lengthways, as the motorway services did it when Dad stopped there on viewing-deck Sundays. You sit. You eat. It tastes of every Sunday, and it goes into you warm. Gain 4 Vigour. Note the codeword FED.

Behind the counter the Chef counts aloud, a number for every forkful you take. "Seventy. Seventy-one."

At the nearest tables, the Delayed have stopped chewing. Their heads have turned towards you. Their forks hang in the air.

The Chef slides a second plate across the counter. Fuller than the first. Steam curls off it. He leaves small prints of frost on the rim.

"On the house," he says. "There's always more."

Rule 4 comes back to you from the Handbook. *Do not eat or drink airside after midnight.*

*If Sam is with you,* he hasn't touched a thing. He's been on the next stool all along, watching every mouthful. He takes your wrist. "Don't," he says.

The second plate smells better than the first.

If you eat the second plate, turn to {D04}.

If you push it away, turn to {F19}.
D04:
Just a bit. To be polite.

You pull the second plate over. The Chef nods. All along the queue behind you, the Delayed nod with him.

Halfway through, you go to stand up, and you can't. You aren't stuck. You're settled. Your legs are heavy and a long way off, and when you look down the plate is full again.

*If Sam is with you,* he's saying your name. It's getting further away. You'll answer him after this mouthful.

Your sleeves go grey. Your boarding pass curls and yellows beside the plate. Under the hum of the fridges, the Chef counts, and somewhere in the hundreds he says a number and nods at you, and moves on.

Much later, someone new stands at the edge of the tables, tired and hungry, sniffing the air.

You raise your fork, in greeting.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {F15} and choose again.
F17:
You leave the trays where they are.

The smell stays with you. It thickens, richer, rounder, sitting on your tongue. Whatever you last ate, your body has forgotten it, and it picks this moment to tell you. The tables tilt. The floor slides left, and back. Lose 1 Vigour.

You catch yourself on the edge of a table. The grey woman eating at it slides her plate towards you.

*If Sam is with you,* a chip from her plate is already on its way to his mouth. You catch his wrist. He drops the chip and pulls free, hard. "Fine." But his tray goes back on the stack. Note the codeword CARE. *If you also have TRUCE,* he nods at the counter. "I'd have had seconds," he says. "Just so you know."

Behind the counter, the Chef has stopped counting. That's what you notice first: the quiet where the numbers were. He leans across the counter towards you, and his breath smells of gravy and cold storage.

Turn to {F19}.
F18:
You hold up the voucher. *VALID UNTIL DEPARTURE.* It's gone soft from your pocket.

The queue stops shuffling. "Ah," says the Chef. "A voucher customer."

He takes it by one corner, stamps it with a rubber stamp so old the date has worn off, and tears it in half.

Then he makes you a sandwich without asking what you want, and wraps it in a sheet of paper from under the counter. Typewriter letters, the same as the Handbook's. The ragged edge of a torn-out page sticks out of one end of the parcel.

He passes it over. As he does, he leans in, close enough that his hat brushes your hair, and stops counting.

"Don't eat the sandwich."

Then he straightens, nods to the next grey face in the queue, and ladles. "Eighty-one," he says. "Eighty-two."

Cross off the VOUCHER. Note the LAST PAGE on your Adventure Sheet.

You walk away from the counter. You don't run; running would be rude, and rude feels dangerous here.

Past the dead tills, onto carpet, back into the perfume. Under the arch you unwrap the sandwich, drop it in a bin, and smooth the page out against a mirrored pillar.

*If Sam is with you,* he holds the other corner down for you, and keeps watching the Food Court.

Turn to {F14}.
F19:
The Chef lays his white fingertips on the counter, one at a time. Up close you can read his badge: CHEF, and nothing else.

"You want the page," he says. "Everybody does."

He touches the breast pocket of his uniform. A folded square of paper shows above the piping, typewriter letters on it, faded and old. It could be the torn-out page of the Handbook. It could be a menu.

"I'm reasonable," he says. "I'll take a trade."

He counts the options off.

"The memory of your father's voice. Only the sound of it. How he said your name. I'd keep it somewhere nice." One. "Or blood. Enough to sign with." Two. "Or nothing, of course. You can always offer nothing." He folds down a third, slowly. "People do."

Behind you, the queue has stopped. At the tables, the forks have stopped. Every grey head is turned your way.

The Chef waits. His eyes flick once to the swing door behind him, the kitchen, and back, so fast you might have imagined it.

If you give him the memory of Dad's voice, turn to {F21}.

If you give him blood, turn to {F22}.

If you give him nothing, turn to {F23}.
F21:
"His voice," you say. "Fine."

The Chef reaches across the counter and lays two fingers against the side of your head, just above your ear. They're so cold they burn. He draws them away slowly, a magician finding a coin, and holds them to his own ear.

He closes his eyes. For a second his mouth goes soft.

"*Kite,*" he says. "Oh, that's lovely."

In his mouth, it's only a word.

You go looking for it. The car in the rain. The viewing deck. The Sunday calls you let go to voicemail. *Every gate's a door, Kite.* You have the words. You have his mouth, the gap in his teeth, the tilt of his head. The sound is gone.

*If Sam is with you,* he sees your face. "He said it as a question," he says quickly. "*Kite?* Up on the viewing deck, every time a plane went over. In case you'd gone with it."

You say it yourself, *Kite*, to hear it. It comes out in your own voice.

The Chef presses the folded page on you. Note the codeword FORGOT. Note the LAST PAGE on your Adventure Sheet.

You don't remember leaving the Food Court. There's carpet under your feet, then the dead tills, then the perfume, and the page is open in front of you.

Turn to {F14}.
F22:
"Blood," you say.

The Chef nods, as if you've ordered sensibly. He lays an order pad on the counter, the old kind with carbon sheets, and beside it a carving knife, wiped clean.

"Your name," he says. "In your own ink."

You nick the pad of your thumb. It doesn't bleed enough. You do it again, deeper. Then you write.

Your name is longer than you remember. Each letter takes more than you think it will, and by the end you are shaking and the pad is spotted red, and there it sits under *ORDER* and above *TABLE 0*, going brown. Lose 4 Vigour.

Far away, out in the terminal, a pen scratches. One letter, firmly made. Add 1 to your Claim.

The Chef tears off the top sheet and pushes it onto the spike by the till, onto dozens of others, all brown, all names. He runs one frosted nail down the stack, lips moving, and never reaches the bottom.

He takes the folded page from his breast pocket and tucks it into your bloody fist. "Paid in full," he says. "Mind how you go."

Note the LAST PAGE on your Adventure Sheet.

You wrap the cut in a paper napkin and walk. The Delayed watch you go, forks raised. You don't unfold the page until you're out under the arch, back among the perfume, with a mirrored pillar at your back and the napkin going red.

Turn to {F14}.
F23:
"Nothing," you say.

The Chef doesn't move. Under his breath, the counting starts again.

Behind you, all the Delayed move together, at the tables and in the queue, with a sound like a hundred collars rustling. Grey faces. Forks held halfway. Chairs begin to scrape back.

"Then you'll have to come and get it," says the Chef.

He glances at the swing door behind him. Just once.

You vault the counter. It isn't graceful. Your knee cracks on the steel and you're past him, his frozen nails brushing your sleeve, and grey arms are reaching over the counter after you, slow, then not slow at all.

*If Sam is with you,* he's over the counter a second behind you.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {F25}. If you fail, turn to {F31}.
F31:
They catch you at the swing door.

Grey hands, soft and cold, like gloves left out overnight, and far too many of them. They take your ankles, your bag strap, the hem of your jacket, your hair. They don't pull hard. They pull patiently. They have all the time there is.

One of them strokes your cheek.

*If Sam is with you,* he's on the far side of the swing door, hauling it wide, shouting your name.

You kick and twist. You leave a handful of hair and a strip of sleeve behind and fall through the door on all fours, onto tiles so cold they sting. Lose 3 Vigour.

The door swings shut behind you, and swings, and swings. On every swing you see grey faces on the other side, waiting for it to open.

Turn to {F25}.
F25:
The swing door flaps shut behind you, and the warmth of the Food Court stays on the other side.

The kitchen is cold. Stainless steel, frost furring the edges of the worktops, your breath going up white. Along the back wall stands a row of chest freezers, humming, each labelled on masking tape with a year. *2019. 2004. 1987.* You don't open the 1987 one.

The last one says *1998*.

The lid comes up with a crack of ice. Inside, folded on top as if fresh from the laundry, lies a uniform. Navy. Red piping. Larkvale wings. It's your size, frozen stiff, with a name badge.

*If you are his son:* The badge says STEWARD, and beneath it, your name.

*If you are his daughter:* The badge says STEWARDESS, and beneath it, your name.

*If neither:* The badge says CREW, and beneath it, your name.

Under the uniform, in a plastic sleeve gone white with frost, is a yellowed sheet. You scrape it off with your thumbnail. *PASSENGER MANIFEST. LV 137. 1998.*

The names run down in seat order. Every one has a single blue line through it. You scrape further, a line at a time, counting under your breath. The nail tears. You keep going. A hundred and thirty-seven.

One name is clean. Seat 1A. Your father's. Beside it, in pencil: *DID NOT BOARD.*

*If you do not already have the LAST PAGE,* there's a torn page frozen to the inside of the lid. You breathe on it and peel it away, one corner missing. Note the LAST PAGE on your Adventure Sheet. Whatever he keeps in his pocket, it was never this.

*If Sam is with you,* he stands with his back against the swing door, both hands flat on it, and doesn't once look at the uniform. "Hurry up," he says, to the steel.

Behind you, the swing door creaks against its hinges. You don't wait for it. You hit the bar of the fire door at the back with your hip, and come out, somehow, among the perfume counters, with the page stiff and cold against your chest.

Turn to {F14}.
F27:
The pods stand in a row along the windows: white capsules with soft blue lights, thin mattresses, sliding doors. They hum. Beyond the glass the apron is dark, the runway lights a long dotted line going nowhere.

You haven't slept since the other airport. Your eyes sting when you blink, and the hum of the pods gets into your back teeth.

*If Sam is with you,* he sits on the edge of the pod nearest the glass. Window, obviously. You look at him properly for once: the grey under his eyes, his arms hanging between his knees. "Ten minutes," he says. "Please. I've done enough nights. I'm owed ten minutes." He's already folding his arms, the way Dad did in front of the television.

On the side of the pod, a printed sticker: *REST UNTIL BOARDING.* Rule 6, from the Handbook: *Do not sleep airside.*

The blue light is soft. The mattress is deep.

If you lie down for ten minutes, turn to {D09}.

If you refuse and get moving again, back towards the counter (*if Sam is with you,* he gets up too, slowly), turn to {F15}.
D09:
Ten minutes. You lie down, and the blue light goes soft at the edges, and you tell yourself you'll keep one ear open.

You wake at the gate.

Gate 14. The hard plastic seats bolted in a row. Your bag at your feet. Above the desk, the board: *LV 137. DELAYED.* The clock beside it says 11:52pm.

For one long, sweet moment, you think none of it happened.

Then you look down at your hands. Thin. Spotted. The knuckles swollen. You push a hand through your hair, and it comes away white.

*If Sam is with you,* further along the row, someone sits with his head bowed and earbuds in, the wires gone yellow. The board clatters. He takes one earbud out. "Typical," he says. You don't recognise his voice.

At the far end of the concourse, the tall passenger holds up its sign. You can read it from here now. It's finished.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {F15} and choose again.
